content_voiceover: This algorithm separates erythrocytosis, an increased erythrocyte concentration that includes relative causes like hemoconcentration or Gaisbock syndrome, from true polycythemia, an increased red cell mass. Work-up starts with serum EPO and JAK2 V617F. If EPO is high, that argues against polycythemia vera and points toward secondary causes: aberrant EPO production from hepatocellular carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, uterine cancer, adrenal adenoma, or Cushing syndrome; or chronic hypoxia from COPD, sleep apnea, pulmonary hypertension, cyanotic congenital heart disease, hypoventilation, high-oxygen-affinity hemoglobinopathy, or high altitude. If EPO is normal or low, test JAK2 V617F — if positive, that essentially confirms polycythemia vera, since JAK2 V617F is found in over ninety-five percent of PV. If negative, reflexively test for JAK2 exon 12 mutations, which are found in most of the remaining JAK2-negative PV cases with an isolated erythrocytosis phenotype. If exon 12 is also negative, proceed to bone marrow biopsy; findings there combined with the EPO level differentiate familial PV or PFCP with low EPO, familial erythrocytosis with normal EPO if the biopsy is unremarkable, or MPN-unclassifiable if the biopsy shows myeloproliferative changes with normal EPO. This algorithm is a favorite board question because it forces you to sequence JAK2 testing correctly — V617F first, then exon 12 if negative — before invoking bone marrow biopsy.
keypoints: JAK2 V617F(+) in >95% of PV — test first
JAK2(-) with high suspicion → test exon 12 mutations next
High EPO → screen for tumor (RCC, HCC) or chronic hypoxia
BM biopsy reserved for JAK2(-) cases to sort PV-mimics
keypoint_voiceover: Key points on the polycythemia work-up. Erythrocytosis means increased red cell concentration, while true polycythemia means increased red cell mass. JAK2 V617F is positive in over ninety-five percent of polycythemia vera, so test it first. If negative, move to JAK2 exon 12 mutations before considering bone marrow biopsy. A high serum EPO should prompt a search for a tumor producing EPO or a chronic hypoxic condition. Bone marrow biopsy is reserved for JAK2-negative cases to distinguish familial PV, familial erythrocytosis, and MPN-unclassifiable.
